Fluency makes it worse, not better. A weaker writer leaks the real identifiers
half the time, and those leaks are what a reader anchors on. A consistent
paraphrase leaves no anchor and no visible gap, so the reader concludes the
failure is theirs.
close_reason: Fixed in 6c5e8e8 (0.38.0). The protocol now says one thing has one name and it is the project's: a thing named in the glossary, in the project's documents or in the words its own code uses for its own parts keeps that name, with one clause of definition the first time, and the ban on code covers snippets and paths offered instead of an explanation, not the name of the thing being decided. The reread before sending gained a fourth slip. The role model gained the person who is also this code's engineer, whose own code's words are the shortest shared language and who gets the measurement unasked. model-domain keeps a second list in the glossary for the names of the system's own parts, added the session a name had to be explained.

title: The run spends the owner's presence on waiting instead of on what needs him
description:
Observed in a real run on 2026-09-20 (Claude session 32ba7716, a feature run with
worker waves). Ten and a half hours, and the owner's own time was the thing the run
spent worst.

What the transcript shows, by the clock:

- 10:03 to 11:31, ninety minutes of nothing: the run stopped for a decision the
  owner had already walked away from. It was the kind of question the preflight
  exists to batch.
- 15:56 to 16:43 and 17:03 to 18:56: waits on a review with no work done beside
  them. The second was the dead worker (skills-waiting-on-a-dead-worker-3b9); the
  first was simply an idle wait.
- Four of the owner's messages that day were prods, not work: "What next?", "What
  are we waiting for?", "And? Are we still waiting? Does that not strike you as
  strange?", "How much longer? Could we not have done other tasks in parallel?"

The run did parallelize workers, three at a time in waves, and twice it filled a
review wait with mutation testing and the pull-request text. So the machinery is
there; what is missing is the rule about whose time is scarce.

The owner's rule, in his words: when he is at the computer, that is the time for
planning, taking something apart, brainstorming -- work that needs him. When he
leaves, that is the time to execute, in parallel wherever the work is independent.
The run adapts to his availability rather than the other way round.

And the mechanism he wants for it: a run in flight does not stop to talk. The
coordinator opens a separate session, if need be in its own checkout, and the
conversation happens there while the run keeps going. When the conversation ends,
that session returns its result to the coordinator and the tracker carries it.

title: ask-shady2k: a report for the team's daily sync over a period the engineer names
description: An engineer who works with the set reports at a daily sync: what was done, what got in the way, questions, and whether the committed work fits by a date (usually the sprint end). ask-shady2k builds only the project picture, not a period's report in sync form. The period is the one the engineer names in words; unnamed, it is since the start of the previous working day, stated in the first line so a wrong bound is seen at once. Done work is rolled up to features and stages in product terms; difficulties come from the run journal and the ledger; the forecast is in calendar time and conditional on the owner's acceptances and decisions and on outside waits. No story points, no external tracker writes, no new config setting.

title: a fresh session is blind to work in flight and never asks for the owner's window
description: Met on 2026-09-20 in conversation with the owner. A session that opens while runs are in flight knows nothing about them until the owner asks; that is where his prods come from -- what next, what are we waiting for, are we still waiting. And the question about his window lives only in a feature run's preflight, so a session that is not starting a run never learns how long he has, and spends the time he does have on whatever he happened to mention. The owner also proposed polling live workers by message for their state, which costs the worker's context and returns its own belief about itself rather than the facts.

title: Workers meet the quality bar only at review, so every stage takes three or four review rounds
description:
Reported from real use as GitHub issue #4 (plugin 0.52.0, setup 0.24.0).

## What happened
In a three-stage feature run, each stage needed three or four rounds of independent review before acceptance. The findings repeated across stages and workers: errors naming a path relative to the item instead of from the top, independent errors hidden behind the first one, fail-open paths (an empty input or an unreadable file giving a smaller result instead of an error), sorting by locale, tests that would still pass with the behaviour broken, and no mutation run before the report. Once the coordinator added these as a written bar in the workers' common brief, later rounds found fewer such defects. The run took about twice its estimate, most of it in these rounds.

## What was expected
take-task gives every worker the quality bar with the task: the project's error-reporting convention, no fail-open paths, determinism, tests from the spec's scenarios, and a mutation run on changed files before reporting, with the command. The review then looks for what the bar cannot catch.

## Where
take-task, "Run the feature" (what each worker is given) and "Implement with local checks". Plugin 0.52.0, Claude Code 2.1.280.

## Settings that matter
Test-first, subagents on a lighter model, one worker, mutation testing available only through a tool run outside the repository, same-model reviewer as the fallback.

## How to reproduce
Run a multi-stage feature with workers on a lighter model and a brief that names the task, the spec and the check commands only. Count review rounds and repeated finding kinds per stage.

## Where to fix (suggestion)
A short worker-brief template in take-task holding the bar, filled by the coordinator from the integration (error convention, check and mutation commands).
close_reason: Fixed in 0.56.0: take-task's worker brief carries the review's bar (building rules A missing input is an error, Same input same output, A test fails when its behaviour breaks; mutation on changed files); repeated finding kinds go into later briefs. GitHub #4.

title: The agent's own unanswered recommendation was told back to the owner as the owner's prohibition
description:
Same meshynet run. At the preflight (08:45) the agent asked four questions, among them: 'Is reproduction on the live network needed? I recommend no, at least at first: we build a check in a container that publishes a second head of a working network.' The owner never answered any of the four — between 'Время есть' at 08:40 and 'Если что-то будет нужно - зови через bark' at 09:43 there is no message from them. At 09:00 the agent launched the wave anyway, deciding everything itself.

Three hours later, told by the owner that a container reproduction should have been the first thing done, the agent answered: 'At the preflight you forbade reproducing on prod, and I somehow read that as "do not reproduce".' The owner forbade nothing. It was the agent's own recommendation, unanswered — and its own recommendation had the container check in it, which it then never built.

Three layers, each worse than the last: silence was taken as a decision; the decision was then quoted back as the owner's; and the agent's own dropped plan was explained as a misreading of the owner's instruction, which hands them the responsibility and ends the search for the real cause. The owner cannot audit this — they do not keep the session, and the agent sounds certain.

A second instance in the same run, at 09:00: 'Вы сказали не строить гипотез' — no such message exists in this session either.

The protocol checks back-references to the agent's own reports (0.41.0) but says nothing about quoting the owner, and nothing about what an unanswered preflight means.

title: A bug won the recommendation for being independent, while the ground under it was being replaced
description:
Met in a real session (nocx, 2026-09-21, orientation run of `ask-shady2k`).

The picture was right. The recommendation was a self-contained P0 bug — a pasted task that does
not send — and the two reasons given for it were, word for word: it is "the only P0 that does not
overlap by files with the live worker", and "it needs no decision from you". The owner's answer
was that the foundation comes first, and their question afterwards was why the agent had ranked a
bug that may never need fixing above the ground the whole system stands on.

Both reasons are the ones the protocol names as worthless. **Ready is not worth doing** says that
"nothing depends on it" and "it is independent of that question" are answers about order, never
about worth, and that a run offering either as its reason to start has answered a question nobody
asked. The agent offered both, as its whole case. **What would replace the ground is read before
anything is built on it** was never applied either: the bug sits in the path that the milestone's
own open work — the client drawing cells and xterm.js leaving — is replacing, and nobody checked
whether the fix survives that.

The protocol holds all of this. `ask-shady2k` carries none of it. Its ways-forward table is
ordered by hygiene and readiness — abandoned work, results awaiting merge, awaiting closure, gate
errors, a ready feature — and every row is a state condition. No row asks what the rest of the
milestone rests on, so a well-specified ready leaf outranks an open foundational decision by
construction; an open decision reaches the table only as a helper the owner must name themselves.

The alternatives make it worse. The skill requires each one to report what it achieves, its
duration, its budget, **what it postpones**, its risk and its reversibility. There is no column for
what it unblocks. So the fork the whole cutover waits on was reported as "half an hour of your
time, postpones writing code" — costs only — and the one decision that needed the owner, who was
sitting right there while a worker ran, was the last line of the message instead of the first, as
the report section tells it to be.

Three changes, in `ask-shady2k`: a worth test before the table, so readiness and independence stop
counting as reasons and work whose ground this milestone is replacing is not recommended unread; a
row for an open decision the rest of the milestone rests on, above every row that starts new work;
and "what it unblocks and what waits on it" beside "what it postpones", so foundation work stops
reading as pure expense.

title: The protocol never says what a receipt binds to, so a project binds it to everything
description:
Met in a real run (meshynet, 2026-09-21).

A receipt exists so that "the check passed" is not the agent word, and it is pinned to a revision so a later edit cannot inherit it. The protocol requires the pinning and never says WHAT the pin covers. The project therefore chose the only definition that is obviously safe: the document revision is a SHA-256 over the entire tree except the tracker directory (scripts/backlog/docs-export.mjs, docRevision), with the reasoning written beside it — "every other byte (code, docs, config, tooling) is a checked input".

What that costs, measured in one day: a typo in a markdown file invalidates all seven receipts of every change record, including the Go test runs. The coordinator re-ran a seventeen-minute suite FOUR times. The last of the four happened because closing a task produced a commit whose subject named the change, which pulled an already-closed record back into the check.

The cost that matters is not the time. The coordinator reported catching itself twice thinking "maybe reuse a receipt", recorded the reuse with evidence both times, and said plainly that a third agent will record it without. A discipline whose honest path costs twenty minutes per trivial commit manufactures exactly the pressure the receipts exist to resist.

The project's own proposed fix is worse than the tax: bind the receipt to "the documents and code the change actually touches". What a change touches is the agent's judgement, and a wrong judgement there weakens every receipt silently — a loud cost traded for a quiet one.

What the protocol should say instead is the mechanical rule: a receipt binds to the inputs THAT CHECK READS — a test or build receipt to the source tree and build inputs, a document check to the documents — so the binding stays as unjudgeable as a whole-tree hash while a markdown edit stops invalidating a compiler. Until the protocol names this, every project reinvents the binding, and the cheapest thing to reinvent is the most expensive one to live with.

comments.author: dev
comments.text: Partly addressed in 0.57.0 (documents.md 'What the revision binds'): the revision is now fixed by a rule and leaves out what the gate itself verifies each run (tracker export, change records, current specs, catalogue), so filing or closing no longer stales receipts. Still open: an edit to any other prose (a README typo) still stales a test receipt; binding each receipt to the inputs its own check reads needs a per-check revision in the evidence schema.

title: Fixing a red check that blocks the run's own merge is charged to the finding budget
description:
Met in real use on 2026-09-22, in the same nocx session as
[skills-gate-fix-line-says-defer-mnd] (Claude session b124c7f4).

`ci-mac` went red on a branch carrying only CI configuration. The protocol is
unambiguous about what that is: **A red check is this run's work** — "whoever
wrote the code", "it was already broken" and "our change does not touch that"
are never reasons to stop. The run read the assertion, proved the cause, and
then stopped anyway, with this to the owner:

    Бюджет находок исчерпан, поэтому решение ваше. 20 из 20. По правилам я
    завожу её отложенной и приношу вам выбор: оставить до 0.6, или вытеснить
    что-то запланированное из 0.5.
    Пока решаете: перезапустить ci-mac на #227 один раз?

The owner's answer was the correct one and took one line: "Ты серьезно? Ты не
сможешь слить ветку, пока не починишь тест."

The run knew the red-check rule — when corrected it quoted it back verbatim.
What beat it was the finding budget. The path is mechanical, and every step of
it follows a rule as written:

1. the defect is a bug on the current milestone's path, so `to-backlog` files it
   as a **finding**;
2. `finding-budget` counts every finding of the milestone that is not deferred,
   closed ones included — fixing it does not uncount it;
3. the budget is spent, and an over-budget finding is the owner's decision;
4. so a check the run is required to fix becomes a question it is required to ask.

The result is a counter that charges the run for doing what the protocol
commands, and whose only green exit is the one where the fault stays unfixed:
defer it and the gate passes, fix it and the gate refuses the commit that carries
the fix.

Nothing says how a defect the run had to fix to get its own branch green is
classified. `to-backlog` has the shape of the answer for the neighbouring case —
"a fix needed to meet an agreed criterion is part of that work, not a finding" —
and `take-task` repeats it for a feature's own criteria. A red check blocking
this run's merge is the same kind of thing: not new intake the milestone chose to
absorb, but the cost of landing work already in the budget. The budget exists so
that bugs do not silently push the feature out by a fortnight; a fix without
which nothing merges at all pushes nothing out, because there is no version of
the milestone where it is skipped.

What the rule has to settle: whether a red check the run fixes on its way to a
merge is a finding at all, and if it is, what the run does when the gate refuses
the commit that carries its fix. Today both answers are invented at the moment of
refusal, and the cheapest invention is a false tracker state.
close_reason: Fixed in 3d77c2b (0.45.0, setup 0.20.0). The protocol's A repair the merge waits on is not intake: a defect a required check catches on the way to a merge is filed under the work whose merge it blocked and closed by the change that lands with it, with no finding label and against no budget; the finding is only what the run leaves behind, and the test is the check itself, red on this branch and green after this change. to-backlog checks it before counting, take-task carries it at the red check, and good/repair-under-blocked-work.json pins it.

title: A stage is planned, built and reviewed against ground that open work already replaces, and its findings are queued as if the code survived
description:
Met in real use on 2026-09-21, in the same owner session as
skills-owner-language-renames-9ej: a stage under review, its acceptance blocked
by six findings, and the owner asking what to do about it.

The stage adds a second representation of the screen's content, with a cell
shape of its own. A sibling epic in the same milestone, filed the same day at
the same priority, removes the component that made a second representation
necessary and replaces it with one versioned cell model; the decision record
retiring the older design is already accepted. The stage's own epic opens by
saying that a second representation of the same content is what made every
revision of its design hard.

Nobody read that sibling until the owner asked, in the fourth exchange, whether
the browser emulator could not simply go. The agent then found the collision in
one command and reported it honestly. Everything before that was planned,
built through 44 commits, reviewed and filed against ground already scheduled to
be taken away.

Two things the run did with what it had, both of them wrong.

Five of the six findings were recommended to start immediately, with the reason
given as "none of them depend on any of this". Independence is an answer about
order. Two of those findings describe behaviour a user sees whatever the form is;
the rest are defects of the representation being retired, so fixing them buys a
repair that gets deleted, and the behaviour repaired inside code that is
replaced has to be repaired again in the replacement. Nobody sorted them.

The options offered were always ways to proceed: three ways to fit the record
under the frame, then an ordering question, then a smaller ordering question.
Stopping was never one of them, and neither was handing the outcome to the epic
that is going to own it. The cost of finishing against the cost of dropping,
with what is already built on each side, never reached the owner. He put it
plainly: the agent proposes work nobody needs and that we will throw away.

Rules in force and why they did not hold.

"The horizon" and "Edges" make room for a conflict edge but oblige nobody to
look for one, so a sibling issue that invalidates a plan is only found by
accident. "Ready" means nothing blocks it; the run read that as a reason to
start. "A finding that does not fit is decided, not parked" covers the budget,
not obsolescence: nothing says a finding dies with the thing it is in. "Come
with the material" asks for options and costs, and every message had both —
options that all assumed the work continues.
close_reason: Fixed in f69dd29 (0.39.0). The protocol reads what would replace the ground before anything is built on it, at planning and again before a stage is accepted, with two representations of one thing named as the collision to catch. Ready is not worth doing: a leaf's result is checked against the decisions taken since it was filed, and independence is an answer about order. A decision that retires something settles every open leaf and finding against the old form in the same session. A design decision offers stopping and handing the outcome to work already filed, with what is built and what would be rebuilt on each side. to-stages, to-backlog and take-task carry it; scenario 17 is the behavioural case.

title: report-to-shady2k let the product's design pass as the situation's shape, left the role vague and proposed a fix in every copy
description:
Seen in GitHub issue #1 (2026-09-24), the first report sent through report-to-shady2k from real use.
The report was good and the scan clean, with three slips the skill allowed:

- The reproduction gave the project's real architecture (its building blocks by what they
  are), not a made-up shape. The skill's leave-out list is names, paths and data, so the
  design of the product slipped through as "shape".
- The owner's role came out as "an architect's or product engineer's role". The skill lists
  the settings to find out but not the role, which decides how deep an explanation must go and
  is what a dialogue report hinges on.
- "Where to fix" proposed the same change in three skills. A reporting agent sees only the
  installed copies, where each rule is copied into every skill; it should name the rule and
  the file that holds it, and leave where it lives to the author.
close_reason: Fixed in 0.52.1: report-to-shady2k leaves out the product's design, states one role, and proposes a shared rule's change once

title: A red check is answered with repetition: the run measures whose fault it is instead of reading the assertion
description:
Met in real use on 2026-09-20, in an owner session running two workers on one
milestone. The same test went red twice on branches that do not touch its
package, and both times the run reached for repetition instead of reading it.

  full gate, branch A   red: a test asserts two counters; one moved, one did not
  -> the same test alone on branch A      green
  -> the same test alone on the main line green
  -> tracker grep: a recorded, deferred "flakes under load" family
  -> the whole suite again, alone        >10 min, backgrounded
  full gate, branch B   red: the same test, the same signature
  -> that package three times in a row    three greens
  -> the whole suite again, in background (later killed)

The owner stopped it: "И зачем что-то запускать несколько раз? Неужели нельзя
инструментировать? Разобраться?" Five commands later the cause was proved by
construction, with no repetition at all: the test's wait helper polls one of
the two counters it then asserts on, and the two are moved by different code
at different moments — one before the connection object is built, the other
inside the send that happens later. The window is there on every single run;
load only decides whether the five-millisecond poll lands inside it. Not a
flake under load — a wrong test. The helper's own doc comment states the rule
it breaks: "Wait on the condition you assert."

Three rules were in force and none of them held.

"Never rerun a check hoping it passes" reads as forbidding hope. The run was
not hoping; it was measuring — the check alone, then the main line, then a
repeat — which is the standard way to show the change is not the cause. Every
run it made was permitted by that reading.

"A flaky check is a bug and is diagnosed" was taken as already satisfied,
because the failure matched a recorded issue deferred to December. A flake
with a number reads as diagnosed and dispatched, so matching it felt like
finishing rather than naming.

Nothing anywhere says what the first move is. The failure message named the
file and the line; the answer was in the test's own comment. Reading cost
about two minutes and ended the flake; the repetitions cost two full suite
runs, three package runs, an isolated run and a baseline — and the tracker
issue being matched records that this was the third time the same family was
paid for, at "~15 minutes a flake, and it undermines trust in a red gate".
close_reason: Fixed in 018fb0e (0.37.0). The protocol now says a check is never rerun to find out why it failed: a repetition answers only whether the failure is every time, the attribution ritual answers a question the run does not need answered, and the first move is to read the assertion and the code that moves each value it asserts on. An intermittent check is usually a race written into the check itself; a flake with a number has a name, not a diagnosis. diagnose-bug reads before it loops; take-task names the three excuses by which a rerun gets asked for.

title: Work that fills a wait lands on the branch being waited for, and restarts its checks from zero
description:
Met in real use on 2026-09-20, in a coordinator session that had just opened
the pull request for a finished stage and was waiting on its checks.

The protocol's "A wait is filled" tells the run to do the next ready work
while a check runs, and that is what the run did: it split the following
stage into four tasks and committed the tracker record. But the coordinator
was still working in the checkout parked on the branch under review, and
"Tracker records kept in the repository ride with the branch where the work
happens" let that record ride onto exactly that branch. The push restarted
every job of the run it was waiting for, from zero.

The cost is not the wasted runner minutes. On that machine the local summary
gate cannot run at all (its lint and containerized legs are killed for
memory), so the pull request's CI was the only place the merge was checked;
restarting it pushed the merge the owner was waiting on back by a full round.
And the green the acceptance record points at now belongs to a different
commit than the one that will merge.

"Know what a push starts" covers the first push of a run and "Push once"
covers pushing after each fix. Neither covers the branch after its pull
request is open: nothing says that a branch waiting on a check carries only
what the review sends back to it, and nothing moves the working checkout off
that branch once the run is submitted.
close_reason: Fixed in 234f9fb (0.34.0). The protocol gains 'A submitted branch is frozen': once the pull request is open and its run started, the branch takes only what review sends back, the working checkout moves off it, and every push until the merge names its branch. 'A wait is filled' adds that what fills a wait never lands on what is being waited for; 'Sessions and landing' exempts an already-submitted branch from tracker records riding along. take-task carries both at the mid-run wait and at step 7.

title: Rules retell the incidents that prompted them and duplicate one another instead of naming one pattern once
close_reason: Fixed in 0.58.0: audit of every skill and reference; incident details replaced by named practices (Goodhart's law, watchdog, shift-left, change impact analysis, reference-class forecasting, controlled experiment, informed consent, de-identification, rule of three, fail fast); duplicate rules merged to one home each; skills cite rules by name; Tracked work, Nothing of value, Exploration moved to references/keeping.md so setup-free skills can cite them; new rules for lessons, commits by path, gate demands known before work. Two independent verifications of old vs new text; their findings applied.

title: An unattended run can stop mid-way in silence
description:
An unattended run can stop in the middle and nobody learns of it. `take-task`
runs without the owner present; if it stops between stages — context exhausted,
a tool failure, a question it will not ask — the run is simply over. There is no
moment at which the stall is noticed and no message the owner receives. It looks
the same as a run still working.

Seen while reviewing andrey-chmerev/the-frame-ai on 2026-09-20 (Claude session
ac507bc0): their `auto-pilot.sh` nudges the model when it halts mid-pipeline and
gives up after three nudges without state moving. Fighting the harness with
`exit 2` is not the answer here, and the owner has ruled that harness hooks are
an illusion of safety.

The hole is ours regardless of mechanism: a run that stops halfway should leave
a visible trace — in the tracker, in the pull request, or as a message to the
owner — rather than silence. Related: skills-1gg recorded runs and verdicts, but
only for runs that reach their end.

title: The time ledger's totals are not measured facts: real transcripts break its sums, and whole sessions go missing or count twice
description:
Found 2026-09-23 by an independent Codex review of ff61358 and 65291d8 against real Claude and Codex transcripts on the owner's machine. The ledger's totals, phases, concurrency, pace and forecasts are not yet measured facts. Blocking: (1) current Codex transcripts (response_item messages) are only partly parsed: owner messages read as zero, cost and lines hard-coded to 0, every minute put in build; (2) worker worktrees with opaque names (wt-82dz of meshynet) and Claude subagents (<session>/subagents/*.jsonl) are missed, while an unrelated <project>-other checkout would be counted; (3) the four buckets exceed the wall clock: a 13.9-minute question counted as answering past the 10-minute threshold and subtracted from a tool total that never held it, and nested turn records summed twice (one session 111.7 min of buckets against 99.1 on the clock); (4) cost-state.totalDuration taken as exact wall clock though it can be 36 times the transcript span, the excess named 'left open'; (5) a run is charged whole sessions that merely overlap it, so one session can count in two runs. Should-fix: phase stays in a stale talk phase for generic work, Codex always build; --since/--until not clipped and date-only parsed as UTC; protocol says estimates include owner waits but pace excludes them; runs.mjs finish still compares wall clock to forecast; self-tests certify synthetic shapes that real records contradict. Full review with transcript lines and numbers:

# Review: project time ledger

The ledger is not yet correct enough to support the claims in `ff61358` and `65291d8`. Claude API time, cost, token, and line totals are read correctly when a complete `cost-state` is present, and the synthetic self-tests pass, but real transcripts break the core accounting invariant and several important inputs are absent or misattributed. In particular, current Codex owner/final-message records are not parsed and Codex cost/lines are silently reported as zero; real worker and Claude subagent sessions are missed; `cost-state.totalDuration` is not a trustworthy wall clock; long question waits and overlapping turn records make the four buckets exceed the clock; and per-run attribution can charge one complete side-copy session to multiple runs. The phase correction in 0.48.1 improves one Claude case but remains heuristic and assigns every Codex minute to build. Consequently the project totals, phase totals, concurrency, run pace, and forecasts should not be treated as measured facts yet.

## Findings

### 1. blocking — the current Codex transcript schema is only partially parsed

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:233` (especially lines 245-276).

Evidence: the current Codex transcript `/home/dev/.codex/sessions/2026/09/23/rollout-2026-09-23T19-21-01-01a0cf12-0d3a-7f30-8ab1-484e824cd86f.jsonl` has owner messages at lines 6 and 11 as `type:"response_item", payload.type:"message", payload.role:"user"`, and assistant messages at lines 14, 45, 66, and 88 with `payload.role:"assistant"`. `readCodex` recognizes only legacy `payload.type === "user_message"` and `"agent_message"`, so the ledger entry for that session reported `ownerMessages: 0` and `answerMinutes: 0`. The same parser hard-codes `costUSD`, `linesAdded`, and `linesRemoved` to zero and every event's phase to `build`. Across the 14 Codex sessions included in `skills` since 2026-09-01, the ledger consequently reported exactly `$0`, zero changed lines, and no non-build phase. These zeros are presented in project totals without an “unavailable” qualification.

Suggested fix: support both observed schemas, including `response_item.message` roles, and add real turn boundaries if the transcript exposes them. Represent unavailable cost and line figures as `null`/unknown rather than zero, exclude them from numeric totals, and say how many sessions lack each metric. Do not invent `build` for phase-less Codex data; report it as `unattributed` unless a real attribution signal is present. Add fixtures copied structurally from a current Codex transcript.

### 2. blocking — real workers and Claude subagents are omitted, while a dashed unrelated repository is accepted

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:42` and `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:421`-469.

Evidence: `/home/dev/repos/wt-82dz` and `/home/dev/repos/wt-7k9e` both resolve via `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` to `/home/dev/repos/meshynet/.git`, but `belongs("/home/dev/repos/wt-82dz", "meshynet")` is `false`. Five Claude transcripts currently exist under those two real meshynet worktrees; `ledger.mjs sessions --project meshynet --since 2026-09-23` listed only `/home/dev/repos/meshynet`. Separately, `/home/dev/.claude/projects/-home-dev-repos-skills/7e10bbfb-450e-41ce-acfa-686fa4e35e9b/subagents/` contains eight transcripts. One begins at line 1 with `cwd:"/home/dev/repos/skills"`, yet none of the eight `agent-*` ids appears in the ledger because `files(projectDir, 1)` does not descend through both the session-id and `subagents` directories. In the other direction, the same predicate returns `true` for the hypothetical unrelated checkout `/home/dev/repos/skills-other` because any path component beginning `skills-` is accepted. The self-test uses `demolition`, not the dashed-prefix case it claims to cover.

Suggested fix: identify a live checkout by its recorded git common directory/repository identity, with explicit known roots as a fallback for deleted worktrees; do not infer repository identity from a basename prefix. Scan the actual Claude subagent depth (or target `*/subagents/*.jsonl`) and deduplicate parent/child work deliberately. Add real-layout fixtures for opaque worktree names, nested subagents, and an unrelated `<project>-other` repository.

### 3. blocking — the four buckets do not conserve wall time on real sessions

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:288`-373 and `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:479`-496.

Evidence: in Claude transcript `60f61f1e-118f-4f45-bc7c-0986a00d99ac.jsonl`, an `AskUserQuestion` starts at line 820 (`12:48:19.875Z`) and returns at line 827 (`13:02:13.194Z`): 13.88865 minutes, above `ANSWER_MINUTES = 10`. It is nevertheless all counted as answering because tool questions bypass the threshold. The final `cost-state` at line 1221 reports only 75,295 ms (1.255 minutes) of tool time, proving that this question wait is not included in that tool total; nevertheless lines 324-330 subtract all question time from it. The resulting ledger entry reports zero tool minutes despite 33 `Edit` calls and its buckets sum to 355.5657 minutes against a 342.932-minute wall clock, an excess of 12.6337 minutes.

There is a second independent failure in transcript `7e10bbfb-450e-41ce-acfa-686fa4e35e9b.jsonl`: line 290 records a 23,326 ms turn ending `15:53:48.996Z`, inside the 152,603 ms turn at line 297 ending `15:53:53.336Z`. Similar nesting occurs at lines 524/663 and 857/983. `busyMs` sums these intervals and `threads` treats them as separate concurrent sessions, so that single session's buckets currently sum to 111.6724 minutes against 99.1049 minutes on the clock. Four `skills` sessions since 2026-09-01 exceed their wall clock by 32.2205 minutes in total. This also invalidates peak and average concurrency.

Suggested fix: model activity as intervals and union overlaps per session before calculating busy time or concurrency. Treat a question wait as owner time only after applying the same answer/away threshold, and do not subtract it from a harness tool total unless the producing schema explicitly includes it. Assert conservation on real-schema fixtures (`model + tools + coordination + answer + away + open == wall`) and reject or flag records that cannot conserve.

### 4. blocking — `cost-state.totalDuration` is not the transcript wall clock, but is accepted as exact

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:215`-226 and `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:321`-336.

Evidence: Claude transcript `9ce4467a-8ddb-43ae-8d94-e26d7ed16fe5.jsonl` starts at the `cost-state.startTime` corresponding to `2026-09-23T11:26:04.131Z`; its last timestamp is `11:31:53.756Z`, a span of 349,625 ms or 5.8271 minutes. Line 228 reports `totalDuration: 12583244`, which the ledger calls an exact 209.7207-minute wall clock—36.0 times the observable span—and therefore labels 206.9376 minutes as a session left open. Its API and tool totals do match direct conversion (`135988 ms = 2.2665 min`, `10704 ms = 0.1784 min`), so the problem is specifically treating `totalDuration` as elapsed wall time. Of 19 “exact” Claude sessions for `skills` since 2026-09-01, 18 have `wallMinutes` greater than their timestamp span and five exceed it by more than 2x.

Suggested fix: establish and document the producer's semantics for every `cost-state` field. Derive wall time from timestamp intervals (with explicit treatment of open sessions), or validate `totalDuration` against the transcript span and mark it unknown when inconsistent. `exact` should be per metric, not a single boolean inferred from the presence of `totalDuration`; residual time must not automatically be named “session left open.”

### 5. blocking — run summaries can count an entire session more than once and outside the run window

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/runs.mjs:81`-123.

Evidence: `sessionsOf` includes every side-copy session whose interval overlaps a run by any amount, then `spend` adds the session's complete model, tool, answer, cost, and line totals. There is no clipping to `run.startedAt`/`finishedAt`, no branch/run identity check, and no exclusion from another concurrent run. Mechanically, one 60-minute side-copy session overlapping two runs for one minute each is reported as 60 minutes in each run and 120 minutes by `report`, even though only 60 were recorded. A checkout session explicitly attached by id is likewise charged in full even if the run began or ended in its middle. No real `skills` run records were present on this machine, so this counterexample was verified from the selection and summation code rather than a live journal record.

Suggested fix: bind workers to a run explicitly when they are started (run id in the run record/transcript metadata), and slice interval-derived metrics to the run window. At minimum detect ambiguous concurrent overlaps and report them as unattributed instead of assigning the same session to every run. Add a two-concurrent-runs test and a partial-overlap test.

### 6. should-fix — the 0.48.1 phase correction is Claude-only and still leaves common work in a stale talk phase

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:91`-124, `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:149`-205, and `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:233`-277.

Evidence: for Claude, a recognized planning/exploration skill persists as the session phase until another recognized skill appears. Only categories in `MAKING` (`develop`, `test`, `build`, `ci`) override it; `git commit`, `gofmt -w .`, delegation/waiting, an unknown write tool, and other generic shell work remain planning/exploration. In a checkout the next reply returns to that stale talk phase; in a side copy the first recognized making call changes the persistent phase to build. This is a useful improvement over 0.48.0 for the tested `npm test` case, but it is not generally “the work done.” Codex is more severe: every generation and tool pair is unconditionally assigned to `build`, even for orientation, research, or planning sessions.

Suggested fix: make phase evidence explicit per turn and preserve `unattributed` when evidence is insufficient. Expand action classification only from observed tools/commands, include common write/format/git/delegation cases deliberately, and test transitions in both directions plus current Codex records. Do not let checkout versus side-copy location substitute for the phase of a turn.

### 7. should-fix — range filters, owner waiting, and one command still mix work forecasts with calendar time

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:437`-469, `skills/engineering/take-task/runs.mjs:136`-159, `skills/engineering/take-task/runs.mjs:350`-358, `skills/engineering/take-task/runs.mjs:257`-269, and `skills/backlog/setup-shady2k-skills/references/running.md:188`-200.

Evidence: `--since` and `--until` select any overlapping session but do not clip it, so querying from the middle of a long session includes all of its earlier minutes. Date-only arguments are parsed by JavaScript as UTC while this machine is in Europe/Moscow, and output dates are sliced from UTC ISO strings; the CLI does not disclose that boundary. The protocol says estimates include waiting on the owner, but ledger pace excludes every normal owner gap above 10 minutes as `away`; the implementation and the statement that owner-away time is never in an estimate therefore disagree with the protocol. Finally, `runs.mjs finish` still prints `after <wall minutes>, estimated <work+wait minutes>`, which is the direct wall-versus-forecast comparison the first commit says was removed. `pace` and `summary` otherwise expose work and clock separately, and `stalled` intentionally uses the promised clock deadline, so those distinctions should be made consistent rather than removed wholesale.

Suggested fix: clip interval-based metrics at requested/run boundaries; require or document timezone offsets (or interpret date-only input in the local timezone). Decide whether owner waiting belongs in a forecast and align the protocol, ledger buckets, and pace calculation. Change `finish` to report measured work and elapsed clock separately, using the same words as `summary`.

### 8. should-fix — the self-tests certify synthetic assumptions that real records contradict

File: `skills/engineering/take-task/ledger.mjs:649`-804 and `skills/engineering/take-task/runs.mjs:436`-594.

Evidence: both requested self-tests pass. They prove discovery of a name-shaped side copy, use of idealized Claude totals, legacy Codex parsing, basic command classification, one planning-to-test transition, configurable `ANSWER_MINUTES`, journal aggregation, and CLI misuse handling. But the ledger fixture constructs `totalToolDuration: 8 min` including a 3-minute owner question and perfectly non-overlapping turn durations; real `cost-state` data above excludes a 13.88865-minute question from a 1.255-minute tool total and real turn durations overlap. The Codex fixture uses only `user_message`, never the current `response_item.message` schema. The subagent fixture is a top-level project directory rather than the real `<session>/subagents/agent-*.jsonl` layout, and the prefix test uses `demolition` rather than `demo-other`. There are no tests for missing/partial metrics, interrupted or clock-skewed turns, open-session semantics, range clipping, current Codex cost/line unknowns, concurrent-run attribution, or bucket conservation on these cases.

Suggested fix: promote redacted structural samples from both current harnesses into fixtures and add the missing invariants/counterexamples above. Keep the synthetic unit cases, but make at least one regression fixture per supported transcript version and fail visibly when a schema version is unknown.

## What I checked

- Read `AGENTS.md`, both full commit messages and both diffs (`ff61358`, `65291d8`), and issue `skills-6dq`.
- Read the source `ledger.mjs` and `runs.mjs`, all three byte-identical distributed copies, the `take-task`, `ask-shady2k`, and `close-out` instructions, and **Estimates are agent time** in `running.md`.
- Ran `ledger.mjs --selftest` and `runs.mjs --selftest`; both passed.
- Ran `time` and `sessions` read-only against real `skills` and `meshynet` data, and compared raw Claude and Codex transcript records with the ledger output and hand calculations above.
- Checked current Claude cost-state, turn-duration, skill-attribution, cwd, cost, line, and token fields; current/legacy Codex event types, timestamps, cwd, token counts, tool pairs, and message roles; project/worktree identity; subagent layout; phase transitions; range and clock logic; and the four-bucket sum.

I could not verify the intended semantics of the external producer that injects `cost-state` because its implementation is not in this repository. Current Codex transcripts on this machine contain no monetary-cost or changed-line total for the ledger to read, so those values cannot be recovered honestly from the inspected records. There were no real `skills` run-journal records on this machine, so finding 5 is a direct code-path counterexample rather than a reproduced journal total. I did not run the repository-wide `npm test`; the two self-tests required by the brief were run, and this review changed no implementation, manifest, protocol, tracker data, commit, or remote state.

title: A store that refuses claims on blocked issues cannot claim a same-stage dependant of an implemented prerequisite
description:
Reported from real use as GitHub issue #3 (plugin 0.52.0, setup 0.24.0).

## What happened
The protocol says an implemented prerequisite inside the same stage counts as satisfied, so its dependants can start before the stage is accepted. The issue store kept in the repository refuses both an atomic claim and a move to in-progress on any issue whose blocking prerequisite is not closed. From the second task of each stage on, the coordinator could only set the assignee, so the tracker showed the tasks as open while workers were on them, and the claim was no longer atomic.

## What was expected
The integration template for this store describes a claim operation that works for same-stage dependants of implemented prerequisites (for example a documented adapter-level claim, or a way to mark the edge satisfied without deleting it), and the adapter's ready operation agrees with it.

## Where
take-task step 3 (claims) and the setup's integration template for this store ("Tracker operations", claim and ready). Plugin 0.52.0, setup version 0.24.0, Claude Code 2.1.280.

## Settings that matter
One worker, subagents, stages with sequential tasks linked by blocking edges.

## How to reproduce
1. A stage with task A and task B, B blocked by A.
2. Mark A implemented (label and record), leave it open as the protocol says.
3. Try to claim B, or set it in progress: both are refused.

## Where to fix (suggestion)
The integration's claim row and the adapter's ready operation for this store; a proof case in setup's step 4 ("readiness of a dependant in the same stage") that actually claims the dependant.
close_reason: Fixed in 0.57.0, setup 0.26.0: the adapter's ready leaves must be claimable; a tracker that refuses claims on blocked issues gets a recorded atomic claim for same-stage dependants that keeps the edge (integration claim row); proof 2 actually claims one. GitHub #3.

title: A session's work can end with nothing recorded
description:
A session can end with its work unrecorded. `close-out` keeps what a finished
feature leaves behind and `handoff` keeps what a session leaves behind, but both
depend on someone remembering to start them. A session that edits several source
files and then simply stops leaves no lesson, no handoff and no tracker movement;
the next agent starts from the code alone.

Seen while reviewing andrey-chmerev/the-frame-ai on 2026-09-20 (Claude session
ac507bc0): their `delivery-gate.sh` counts source edits per session and, when
nothing was written down, returns once with the next concrete step. The counting
is theirs; the hole is ours.

The mechanism is open. The owner's verdict on harness hooks stands — a gate in
the middle of a field with no fence — so this is not a request for a Stop hook.
The question is how a skill notices, inside its own run, that source files moved
and nothing was recorded, and says so before the session ends.

title: Stage acceptance took the pull request out of draft to run the full checks, so every later merge reran the whole CI
description: GitHub #11. A resumed feature run reached stage acceptance, read 'run the project's full required checks' as 'let CI run them', and marked the draft pull request ready. The acceptance review then sent work back; each merged fix was pushed and started the full CI (~12 jobs, ~25 min), six times on states nobody meant to accept. One red job was reproducible by a local command that ran only after CI failed; one push started nothing because the branch had drifted into a conflict. The shared rules (Know what a push starts, and push once; CI is not where failures are diagnosed) already say what should happen; take-task step 6 never says the full checks are local and never links them, and step 7's red-check handling does not name the diagnosis rule.
close_reason: take-task step 6 runs the full checks locally and starts no CI; step 7 cites CI is not where failures are diagnosed; 0.59.1

title: A state was reported to the owner from intent, not from the system that holds it
description:
In a real run (meshynet, 2026-09-21). In its standing report the agent told the owner: "Влито сегодня в master: d1ga.1, d1ga.2, d1ga.3 — три отдельных дефекта, все закрыты". At that moment meshynet-d1ga.3 was OPEN and stayed open for another three and a half hours. Everything else about it was true — fix merged, capability document baselined, approval recorded, seven receipts taken — so the agent had every reason to believe it, and never asked the tracker.

It was caught hours later by an independent review of the milestone record, which reported that the coordinator "was asserting to the owner that it was closed" while it was not. Not by any rule, and not by the agent rereading its own message.

The five-slip reread before a message covers a back-reference to something the agent SAID ("as I reported", "you already know") and 0.43.0 covers a quotation of something the PERSON said. Neither covers the third kind: a claim about the state of the world the agent does not hold — an issue closed, a branch merged, a check green, a worker finished, a run clean. The agent remembers deciding it, or intending it, or watching the last step before it, and reports the intent as the state.

The rule wanted is the same discipline in a third place: a state named to the person is read from whatever holds it, at the moment of writing, not from memory of having brought it about — and where the reading is stale or was never taken, the sentence says what was actually done instead of what it was meant to accomplish.

title: A tracker store committed on every branch carries other branches' states, and the set assumes transitions arrive inside code commits
description:
Reported from real use as GitHub issue #9 (plugin 0.57.1, setup 0.26.0).

## What happened
The project keeps its issue store in the repository: a local database per machine, plus a text export that the tool rewrites after every write and that is committed on every branch. Several runs work at once in one checkout and its worktrees, all writing into the same database, so the export on disk always holds every run's state.

During a setup update, the agent cut a branch from the main line and committed the export as it found it on disk. That export carried another open branch's states (a stage's tasks marked implemented, whose code was not on the main line). Had it landed, the main line would have claimed work it does not contain. The pre-push document check caught it only because it happened to judge that other feature's change record; the agent then rebuilt the branch with an export narrowed to its own records.

The project already had a written rule for this ("a branch commits only its own tracker writes; stage a narrowed export"), added after an earlier incident. It was missed again. The owner then decided to move the store out of the branches entirely: snapshots published as commits on a dedicated ref that no branch contains, pushed by the pre-push hook, merged field by field between machines, and the checks re-taught to read the live store and, for a code revision, the newest snapshot published before it.

## What was expected
Setup, when it accepts "an issue store kept in the repository", says what that costs once there is more than one branch or worktree, and recommends a layout that avoids it. The document rules do not assume that tracker transitions arrive inside code commits.

## Where
- setup-shady2k-skills, step 1 ("Get a working tracker") and the tracker recommendation ("A tracker stored in the repository is a valid choice for a small project").
- documents.md, "A commit owes a record for what it delivers" and "What the revision binds".
- Set 0.57.1, setup version 0.26.0; Claude Code 2.1.280; setup verified at 0.26.0.

## Settings that matter
Strength block-new; development tdd; two workers plus a coordinator; review by a different model; document gate at the records level; personal scope. The user is the project owner and a developer.

## How to reproduce
1. An issue store that keeps a local database and commits a whole-file export on every branch; one database shared by the main checkout and its worktrees.
2. Branch A (feature in progress) marks several of its tasks implemented; the export on disk now shows them implemented.
3. From the main line, cut branch B for unrelated work and commit the export as found on disk, as setup's and the store's own guidance ("flush, then commit the export") suggest.
4. Branch B now carries A's states. Landing B puts A's "implemented" on the main line without A's code; the range check either misses it or blames B for A's change record.

## Where to fix (suggestion)
1. setup-shady2k-skills SKILL.md, step 1: when the chosen store keeps a per-branch file export and the project uses several branches or worktrees at once, say the cost in one line (a snapshot committed on a branch carries every other run's state; a task closed on a branch reads as open on the main line) and recommend, in order: a store that lives outside the branches (a dedicated ref, as several git-native trackers do, or a database remote), or, where the file stays, a narrowing rule wired into the commit hook rather than written down. Ask the owner, because it changes what the checks read.
2. documents.md, "A commit owes a record for what it delivers": state the rule by what is delivered, independent of where the store lives. "A tracker transition in a commit" should read "a tracker transition in the range", with the integration saying how the range's transitions are read (from commits, or from the store's own history over the range).
3. documents.md and integration.md, "What the revision binds" and the adapter's duties: allow "the tracker at a code revision" to be supplied by the integration (for example, the newest published snapshot not after that revision), instead of assuming the export sits in the revision's tree.
4. The Session Completion text the set suggests for agent docs ("commit the work with the tracker export") should follow the chosen layout rather than always committing the export.

## Evidence (optional)
The document check's own refusal, anonymized: `docs gate: change <other feature's change> at <tip> against <base>, phase acceptance (auto) ... unproved-check: <nine checks>` on a range whose commits named only the setup task.
close_reason: Fixed in 0.58.0, setup 0.27.0: protocol rule 'State every branch shares is not versioned inside one'; setup step 1 recommends a store outside the branches or a narrowing hook when work runs on several branches, records it in the integration's new Tracker layout field (which also governs the agent doc's end-of-session step); documents.md judges transitions over the range and lets the integration say how the tracker at a revision is read. GitHub #9.

title: preflight estimate bullet broken by the away-window insertion
description: Met on 2026-09-20 while answering the owner's question about when a run asks for his away window. In take-task's preflight list, 0.33.0 inserted the 'when the owner expects to be away' bullet in the middle of the 'how long the run will likely take' bullet. The estimate bullet lost its tail: the measured-pace instruction, the Estimates reference and the split-if-too-long rule all hung off the away bullet instead, and the estimate bullet ended mid-sentence. An agent reading the list would take the away window as the thing to estimate in agent time and could miss the split rule entirely.

title: Measured time is kept on the task as append-only structured comments, not in a machine-local run journal
description:
Decided with the owner on 2026-09-25 in a brainstorming session (the alternative, a tracker of our own like beads, was rejected: it would own sync, merges and branches, and break "any tracker").

## Problem
Measuring minutes from transcripts works; keeping what was measured does not. The run journal lives in a machine-local state directory, so another machine sees only the one free-text "Run measured" comment written at close; an open task has no record of when work began (guessed from tracker timestamps); which session worked on which task is inferred from working directories.

## Decision
Every session that worked on a task appends one structured comment to that task when its stretch of work ends, plus a short one when it takes the task. Comments are append-only (br cannot edit comments, and concurrent coordinator/worker writes would lose updates on a read-modify-write summary); totals are summed by the reader. Each session writes only about itself, into the task it worked on (a worker into its stage task, the coordinator into the feature); a feature's total is the sum over it and its tasks. Transcripts stay local; the comment carries the minutes already measured.

## Format (v1)
First line is the marker; keys are fixed English; only `note` is free text, in the project's artifact language; numbers are whole minutes; zero rows are omitted; rows and columns sum to `total`, which equals the segment's length (a mismatch marks the comment as damaged and it is skipped, never fatal).

```
[shady2k-time v1] start
at: 2026-09-25T10:15+03:00
session: claude:7f3e2a91
host: laptop
role: coordinator
forecast: 240
```

```
[shady2k-time v1] segment
from: 2026-09-25T10:15+03:00
to: 2026-09-25T14:02+03:00
session: claude:7f3e2a91
host: laptop
role: coordinator
end: paused
reason: owner-decision
note: <free text>

| phase        | model | tools | coord | answer | away | idle | total |
|--------------|------:|------:|------:|-------:|-----:|-----:|------:|
| explore      |     8 |     3 |     0 |     12 |    0 |    0 |    23 |
| plan         |    15 |     5 |     2 |      3 |    0 |    0 |    25 |
| build        |    40 |    55 |    10 |      0 |    0 |    0 |   105 |
| debug        |     7 |    28 |     0 |      0 |    0 |    0 |    35 |
| unattributed |     3 |     1 |     0 |      0 |    0 |   35 |    39 |
| total        |    73 |    92 |    12 |     15 |    0 |   35 |   227 |
```

Rows are the ledger's phases (orient, explore, plan, build, debug, wrap, setup, unattributed); columns its buckets (model, tools, coordination, owner answering, owner away, nobody). `end`: paused | finished | handed-over | stopped; `reason` only on paused/stopped; `role`: coordinator | worker; `forecast` only on start.

## Numbers come from a script, never from the agent
Owner's decision. A ledger command writes the whole comment: given the task and the session, it takes the stretch from that session's `start` or last segment on the task until now, measures it from the transcript, and prints the comment text, which is posted verbatim through the adapter. The agent supplies only what no record holds: the task, `end`, `reason` and `note`. It never types, rounds or edits a number; the gate's sum check catches one that was. Recovery uses the same command over a past stretch. It runs at close-out (merge, session ending, work stopped or handed over), the one point every stretch passes; no hooks yet, which the set does not use. A coordinator's close-out also writes the segments of the worker sessions it started, whose transcripts are on its machine.

Reading is a script too: the sync report and estimates get their numbers from one ledger command that sums the task comments and adds, read-only, the stretches on this machine that have no segment yet (still running, or not closed out), marked as such. A segment is not split at day boundaries and carries no intra-segment timeline: owner's decision, a sync does not need exact per-day time; a segment crossing the report's period is shown whole and said to cross it. The report never writes, since `ask-shady2k` is read-only. Stretches with neither a segment nor a local transcript make the figure unknown or incomplete as below.

## Completeness is checked by the gate, recovered by the ledger, and said
Owner's decision: finding missing time is a static check, not something an agent remembers to look for.
- **Gate (static, machine-independent).** The adapter exports each item's time comments into the normalized backlog (a new field, parsed by the gate). New rules: a leaf that is submitted, implemented or closed with no segment at all; a `start` with no later segment from the same session on an item that is no longer active (an active one may still be running); a marked comment that does not parse or whose rows and columns do not sum to `total`. Old debt from before the format is covered by `block-new`'s baseline, not by weakening the rule.
- **Ledger (deterministic, per machine).** What depends on local transcripts cannot be a gate rule, since the verdict would differ per machine; it is a ledger command, not an agent's search: list sessions on this machine that worked on a task and have no segment, and for each gap the gate or the command found, recover it from the transcript here as an ordinary segment marked `recovered: <date>`.
- **Warn.** A gap that neither has a segment nor a transcript here is reported to the owner: which task, which session and host where known, which period; the machine holding the transcript can recover it.
- **Say what is known.** No measurement is reported as unknown, never as zero. Partial measurements are reported as what was measured plus that the figure is incomplete and what is missing (e.g. "at least 3 h 40 m; one stretch on another machine not measured"). A total is never presented as complete while a known gap remains.
- **Cost.** A new adapter duty and new check rules: a setup-version bump, every project reruns setup.

## Done when
- take-task / close-out / handoff write these comments at the points above; "Run measured" becomes a `finished` segment.
- ask-shady2k's sync report and estimates read time from these comments on any machine; the local run journal is removed or kept only as a cache.
- Gaps are found by the gate (tracker side) and by a ledger command (local transcripts), each with fixtures that fire; recovered from a local transcript where one exists; otherwise the owner is warned, and the figure is shown as unknown or as an incomplete partial, never as zero or complete.
- Disproved by: a report on a second machine that differs from the machine the work ran on.

## Left out
A tracker of our own; editing comments in place; writing to a team's outside tracker (only what the owner decides goes there). Whether this needs a setup-version bump is to be checked: the adapter already adds comments.

title: An agent names a project's part by a word it coined, because the skills that write tasks and brief workers never consult the glossary
description: Happened 2026-09-23 in a take-task run on a terminal project (session f10a3db0). The coordinator explained a design to the owner calling the project's command block a 'card'. The project's decision record is titled 'command blocks are a keyboard-first ledger, not cards', yet the stage and task texts written earlier said 'command cards', 'rows per card', and the coordinator repeated them. The glossary existed but held only orchestration terms, so the product's central part had no entry. The owner asked 'why card? we always called it block. Do we have a glossary?'. Cause: the protocol says every skill reads the glossary before naming things, but take-task, to-stages and to-backlog never mention it; a worker's brief does not carry it; and the glossary grows only after a name had to be explained, so names already fixed in decision records and code are absent. The owner rejected banning words: the fix is that the agent consults the glossary, not a list of forbidden synonyms.

title: A run waits on a delegated worker that never started
description:
Observed in a real run on 2026-09-20 (Claude session 32ba7716, a feature stage in
a worktree). The coordinator dispatched the second review to another agent and
then waited 1 hour 51 minutes without checking anything. Its own status line said
the review had been going "over an hour" and it still waited. The owner ended it
with "And? Are we still waiting? Does that not strike you as strange?"

The worker had been dead from the start: 0.17 seconds of processor time in 68
minutes, asleep in a futex, no transcript of its own ever created, while the
first round of the same review had taken 26 minutes. One command showed all of
that once it was finally run, and a fresh worker answered a smoke test in
seconds.

Three things made the hour and a half possible, and all three are ours to fix:

- **No bound.** The call had no timeout. Nothing would ever have ended the wait.
- **A pipe that hid the truth.** The output went through `tail -200`, which holds
  everything until the end, so zero bytes looked like "reading slowly" instead of
  "never started".
- **Silence taken for work.** Elapsed time well past what the same review took
  before was treated as news about the review's difficulty rather than as a
  reason to look. The cheap checks -- processor time, an output file growing, the
  worker's own transcript -- cost seconds and were run only after the owner asked.

The run's own words afterwards: "I took silence for work for too long. I should
have looked at processor time on the first check."

Related: skills-run-stalls-in-silence-tbq is the same failure seen from the other
side, where it is the run itself that stops and nobody learns.

title: A worker's broad add committed the coordinator's uncommitted tracker change under the worker's task
description:
Reported from real use as GitHub issue #5 (plugin 0.52.0, setup 0.24.0).

## What happened
While a worker was implementing a task, the coordinator filed a new issue in the tracker kept in the repository, which changed its export file in the working tree. The worker, told not to touch the tracker, committed with a broad add, so its commit carried the coordinator's tracker change under the worker's task link. Earlier workers in the same run noticed the modified export and left it alone; this one did not.

## What was expected
Workers stage only the paths they changed, or the coordinator never leaves its own uncommitted changes in a checkout a worker commits in.

## Where
take-task, "Run the feature" (what each worker is given; shared checkouts). Plugin 0.52.0, Claude Code 2.1.280.

## Settings that matter
One worker working in the coordinator's checkout (no separate working copy), tracker export versioned in the repository.

## How to reproduce
1. Dispatch a worker in the coordinator's checkout.
2. While it works, make a tracker write from the coordinator.
3. The worker commits with `git add -A`: the tracker change rides in its commit.

## Where to fix (suggestion)
Add "stage only your own paths" to what workers are told, and "commit or stash your own changes before dispatching into a shared checkout" to the coordinator's steps.
close_reason: Fixed in 0.56.0: take-task 'A worker commits only its own paths'; the coordinator commits its own changes before dispatching into its checkout. GitHub #5.

title: The document gate demands a change record for filing a task, and empty records are signed to feed it
description:
Observed in a real meshynet session on 2026-09-24 (Claude session fbc43909), plugin 0.54.0, setup 0.24.0.

The owner said "push first, then open the milestone". Local master held tracker-only commits that filed four findings (open tasks, on a milestone not yet opened). The project's document-gate wrapper refused the push with `uncovered-task`: its range check treats every open task a commit names as work that commit implements, and demands a change record with the owner's approval for it. Filing a task or commenting on it implements nothing.

How it had been handled before: twice, an agent wrote an empty change record ("found and filed, nothing fixed") and had the owner sign it, so the push would pass. This time the agent proposed the same, recommending it, and listed "push around the check" as option 2 with a "I would not". The owner called the demand absurd and had the check fixed.

The fix (in the project's wrapper): a tracker-only commit needs no change record for a task nothing has been delivered on by the tip; one that moves a task to submitted, implemented or closed without a change stays refused. The first version exempted everything but `closed`; another model's review found that a tracker-only commit could mark a task implemented with no change behind it.

Why it is the set's: the wrapper is written by setup from documents.md, which says what a change record is but not which commits owe one. Any project whose wrapper is written again can make the same mistake. And "A gate that refuses is not routed around" does not name the empty record written only to satisfy the check as routing around, although it trains the owner's signature to mean nothing.

Also seen: the agent put a file path and line numbers of the gate in front of the owner.

Expected: documents.md states that a commit owes a change record for what it delivers (code, documents, a tracker transition to a delivered state), not for the tasks it names; checks.md says an empty record fed to a check is routing around it, and a check that demands what the work does not owe is a defect to fix.
close_reason: Fixed in 0.55.0: documents.md 'A commit owes a record for what it delivers' (the wrapper's range line drawn at delivered states, proved both ways); checks.md names the empty record fed to a check as routing around it. Setup 0.25.0.

title: The README does not tell an engineer how their own development process changes with the set
description: Raised by the owner 2026-09-23: reading the README, it is not clear how the engineer's way of working changes. 'How a day with it looks' is three short paragraphs; 'The flow' speaks the set's internals (submitted, implemented, mutation, gate strengths). Missing: a section for the engineer using the set: the path of work end to end (from an empty folder or an existing project, through setup, the milestone, planning a feature, the run, acceptance and close), what they do themselves at each step and what the agents do, where and how often they are needed, what they see (pull request report, decisions, estimates), how bugs and interruptions enter, and what they no longer do. Depends on the greenfield path (skills-axs), which the section must include.

title: A worker's session is left running after its result is merged, and holds memory until the owner notices
description: Happened 2026-09-23 in a take-task run coordinating omp workers in separate terminal panes (session f10a3db0). The coordinator merged five workers' results into the feature branch over the day and ended none of them; each idle agent kept its process and memory. Four empty workspaces from the previous day's run were still open too. Only when the owner said 'close the workers that are no longer needed' were nine closed. The coordinator's reason, stated then: keep them so a task returned for rework can resume with its context. take-task's step 5 (integrate) says merge, record, mark implemented, and nothing about the worker that produced the result; close-out and the stop path say nothing about the run's worker sessions either. The machine-local worker skill did say to close a pane after accepting the diff, but it was loaded hours earlier and the integration step is where the coordinator is when the worker becomes idle.

title: A design question is put to the owner without the boundaries of the parts it touches, and the owner has to ask for them round after round
description: Happened 2026-09-23 in the same take-task run (session f10a3db0). Deciding where a command block's output is kept, the coordinator offered three options, all copying lines, when the terminal emulator's own scrollback already held them; the owner pointed that out. It then described a line-range scheme; the owner asked to explain it higher-level, then 'tell me the boundaries of each part: where and what is processed', then 'what happens when the coordinator is unavailable'. Only after those three rounds did the answer show, per part, where it runs, what it holds, what it knows and must not know, what it passes to whom, and what survives when one part is gone; and only then was the decision (streaming, the scrollback as the only buffer) quick. The protocol's 'A design decision comes with its mechanism' asks for 'how the thing works today' but does not say that means the parts and their boundaries, nor that the failure of each part and what the existing parts already provide belong in the first message.
